q: What are the SRE principles from Google's book, and which ones do you apply first in a new team?
p: Embrace risk with explicit SLOs, eliminate toil, monitor what matters, automate, simplicity, release engineering, and blameless learning. Start with SLOs and an incident process since they create shared language and priorities.
cmds: 1. Define 2-3 SLIs per critical user journey
2. Agree SLOs and an error budget policy
3. Set up on-call, severity levels, postmortems
4. Measure toil, pick the top automation target
tip: Do not try to adopt every principle at once. Pick the ones that remove the biggest current pain.
a: The core ideas are that reliability is a feature measured by users, that perfect reliability is the wrong goal because it is expensive and slows change, so I manage risk with explicit targets and error budgets. Other principles are limiting toil so engineers spend time on engineering, monitoring symptoms rather than causes, automating repetitive work, keeping systems simple, treating release engineering as a first-class discipline, and learning from failure through blameless postmortems. In a new team I do not roll out everything. I begin with what creates shared language and decisions: define service level indicators and objectives for the most critical user journeys, agree an error budget policy with product, set up a clear on-call and incident process with severity levels, and start writing postmortems. Once that foundation exists, I measure toil and pick the biggest automation target, and then address capacity, release safety and resilience testing in order of risk.
f: Why is perfect reliability the wrong goal?
What would you do in the first 30 days?

q: How do you decide which services deserve SRE attention and which should stay with the development team?
p: Prioritise by business criticality, user impact, change rate and operational burden. Use readiness reviews and engagement tiers: full SRE support for critical services, consulting and tooling for the rest, and clear criteria to hand back.
cmds: Tier 1: important -> shared on-call + SRE consulting
Tier 2: internal/low -> dev team owns, self-service tooling
tip: A production readiness review is the gate. Services that fail it stay with the dev team until they improve.
a: SRE capacity is limited, so I allocate it where it reduces the most risk. I tier services by business criticality, number of users affected, revenue or safety impact, dependency fan-out, and how operationally painful they are, measured through incident counts, pages and toil. Critical tier services get dedicated SRE engagement, including shared on-call. Other services get lighter touch: consulting, reviews, shared tooling and templates, with development teams owning operations. Before taking on a service, it must pass a production readiness review covering monitoring, SLOs, capacity, rollback, runbooks and documented dependencies. If the service is poor, SRE can give the team a list of improvements and engage only once they are done. Engagements also have exit criteria: when a service is stable and its toil is low, SRE can reduce support and hand operations back, keeping the model sustainable.
f: What is a production readiness review?
When do you hand a service back?

q: What are common failure modes of an SRE team itself, and how do you avoid them?
p: Becoming a ticket-taking ops team, no authority to say no, hero culture, ignoring toil, or being separated from developers. Avoid with an engineering mandate, toil cap, error-budget policy backed by leadership and shared ownership.
cmds: engineering project hours vs ticket hours
tip: If SRE only reacts to tickets, it is just operations with a new name.
a: A common failure is turning into a ticket queue: work arrives from others, nothing gets automated, and engineers burn out. A related one is lacking authority, so SRE raises reliability concerns but cannot slow risky launches because there is no agreed error budget policy with leadership backing. Hero culture is another, where a few people fix everything and knowledge stays in their heads, creating burnout and single points of failure. Teams can also drift apart from developers, so they inherit systems they did not design and cannot change. To avoid these I protect engineering time with a toil cap, track toil and pages as metrics, secure executive agreement on the error budget policy, rotate people through on-call and documentation duties, embed SREs with product teams for design reviews, and make reliability improvements visible work with goals, not invisible heroics.
f: How do you protect engineering time?
What does hero culture cost?

q: What is the difference between availability, reliability, resilience and durability?
p: Availability is the fraction of time the service works; reliability is consistent correct behaviour over time; resilience is the ability to withstand and recover from faults; durability is that stored data is not lost. They need different measures.
cmds: durability: 11 nines = 1 object lost per 10^11 per year
resilience: test via fault injection and failovers
tip: A system can be highly available yet lose data. Durability and correctness need their own SLIs.
a: People use these words loosely, but they measure different things. Availability is whether the service responds successfully when users need it, typically expressed as a percentage of good requests or uptime. Reliability is broader: the service does what it should, correctly and consistently, over time, so it includes latency, correctness and freshness, not only being up. Resilience is the system's ability to absorb faults such as an instance failure or a dependency outage, degrade gracefully and recover quickly, which I validate through fault injection and failover tests. Durability applies to data: the probability that stored information is not lost or corrupted, for example through replication and backups; object stores quote very many nines for it. A service can be available but unreliable, returning wrong results, or available yet not durable if a failure loses writes. So I define separate indicators and targets for each property that users care about.
f: Can a system be available but not durable?
How is availability related to MTTR?

q: What is the difference between monitoring, observability and telemetry, and why does the distinction matter for SRE?
p: Telemetry is the raw data (metrics, logs, traces). Monitoring checks known conditions against thresholds. Observability is the ability to ask new questions of a system and understand unknown failures from its outputs.
cmds: # known unknowns -> monitoring: alert when error_rate > 1%
# unknown unknowns -> observability: slice by version, region, customer, endpoint
tip: High-cardinality, well-structured events let you debug failures you did not predict.
a: Telemetry is simply the data a system emits: metrics, logs, traces and events. Monitoring is the practice of watching specific signals I decided in advance matter, and alerting when they cross thresholds, which is perfect for known failure modes. Observability is a property of the system: whether I can understand its internal state from its outputs well enough to debug situations I did not anticipate. In a distributed system, failures often involve an unexpected combination, such as one customer on one version in one region, so I need rich, high-cardinality context attached to events and the ability to slice and compare dimensions quickly. For SRE this matters because dashboards and alerts for known causes are not enough during a novel incident. I invest in structured events, consistent trace context, service-level instrumentation and fast query tools, so that engineers can form and test hypotheses in minutes rather than guessing.
f: What does high cardinality enable?
Can you have monitoring without observability?

q: How do you write an SLO document that stakeholders actually use?
p: State the user journey, SLI definition and measurement point, target and window, exclusions, error budget policy, owner and review cadence, in one page agreed with product. Link it to dashboards and alerts.
cmds: SLI: 2xx/3xx responses under 500ms at the load balancer / all valid requests
tip: If product has not signed the SLO, it is not an SLO. It is an engineering wish.
a: A good SLO document is short and unambiguous. It names the service and the user journey it protects, defines the indicator precisely, including what counts as a good event, what counts as valid, and where it is measured, for example at the load balancer or from the client. It states the target and the window, such as ninety-nine point nine percent over a rolling twenty-eight days, lists explicit exclusions like planned maintenance and why, and links to the dashboard and alerts that implement it. Crucially, it includes the error budget policy: what the team does when the budget is low or exhausted, agreed in advance with product and engineering leadership. The document has an owner and a review schedule, because targets should be revisited as the product and user expectations change. I get product sign-off, because the SLO is a business decision about acceptable risk, not only a technical number.
f: What belongs in the exclusions?
Who must sign off the SLO?

q: How do you handle SLOs for dependencies, and why does a chain of 99.9% services not give 99.9%?
p: Serial dependencies multiply: three 99.9% services give about 99.7%. Compute the composite, add redundancy or fallbacks for critical paths, and set your SLO below what dependencies allow or mitigate their failures.
cmds: # decide: tighten deps, cache, queue, or degrade gracefully
tip: You cannot promise more availability than your hard dependencies unless you add fallbacks that tolerate their failure.
a: When a request must pass through several components in series, the success probability is the product of each component's availability. Three dependencies at ninety-nine point nine percent give about ninety-nine point seven percent overall, which is roughly a day of downtime in a year, noticeably worse than any single one. So when I set an SLO for my service, I look at my critical dependencies' real performance, not just their promised numbers, and calculate the ceiling. If the target is higher than the ceiling, I have options: reduce the number of hard dependencies in the request path, add caching or stale-serving fallbacks, make calls asynchronous through a queue, or degrade gracefully when a dependency fails. Redundant parallel paths raise availability because both must fail. I also agree on SLOs with dependency owners and monitor their contribution to my error budget.
f: How does redundancy change the maths?
How do you reduce hard dependencies?

q: How do you implement SLOs with Prometheus recording rules and Sloth or OpenSLO?
p: Define SLI ratios as recording rules over multiple windows, compute error budget and burn rates from them, and generate alerts and dashboards from a declarative SLO spec with tools like Sloth or Pyrra to avoid hand-written errors.
tip: Generate rules from a spec. Hand-written multi-window burn rate alerts are easy to get subtly wrong.
a: I start by defining the service level indicator as a ratio of good events to valid events, computed by a recording rule over a short window like five minutes, so downstream queries are cheap. Longer windows, such as thirty minutes, six hours and the full slo window, are derived from it. From those, I compute the error budget remaining and burn rates, then the multi-window multi-burn-rate alerts that page for fast burns and ticket for slow burns. Writing all this by hand per service is repetitive and error-prone, so I use a declarative spec, for example in the OpenSLO format or the Sloth and Pyrra tools, which generate the recording rules, alerts and dashboards consistently. The spec lives in Git alongside the service, is reviewed, and validated with rule linting in CI. I then verify alerts by replaying historical incidents to see if they would have fired at the right time.
f: Why record at a short window?
Why generate rules from a spec?

q: What are common mistakes when setting SLOs?
p: Too many nines, measuring server health instead of user experience, a single average-based SLI, no business sign-off, SLOs no one acts on, windows too short or long, and never revisiting targets.
cmds: SLO 99.999% for a service whose users tolerate minutes of downtime
No policy for when the budget is spent
tip: An SLO nobody uses to make decisions is decoration. Tie it to alerts, release gating and planning.
a: A frequent mistake is aiming for too many nines because it sounds impressive, when users would not notice the difference and the cost and slowdown are large. Another is choosing indicators that measure resource health, like CPU or queue length, rather than what users experience, such as successful and fast responses. Averages hide the slow tail, so percentile or threshold-based latency indicators are better. Teams also write SLOs without product agreement or without a consequence, so when the budget is spent nothing changes, and the SLO becomes decoration. Windows can be wrong: too short makes the number noisy, too long makes it slow to react. Finally, targets get set once and never reviewed, even as the product, traffic and user expectations evolve. I check each SLO against questions: does it reflect user pain, can the team act on it, and does leadership honour the policy.
f: Why avoid too many nines?
What makes an SLO actionable?

q: How do you set SLOs for asynchronous systems like queues, event streams and email delivery?
p: Measure freshness (age of oldest message or end-to-end delay), completeness (messages processed without loss), and correctness, not request latency. Use percentile delay targets and monitor the backlog trend.
tip: Queue depth alone is misleading. Age of the oldest item tells users' real wait time.
a: Asynchronous systems have no request-response cycle to time, so the user experience is about whether work gets done, how soon and whether it is right. I use three kinds of indicator. Freshness or end-to-end latency: the time from event creation to completion, targeted at a percentile, such as ninety-five percent of messages processed within two minutes. Completeness or durability: the share of messages that are eventually processed without loss or unrecoverable failure, tracked by comparing produced and processed counts and dead-letter queue volume. Correctness for results, like valid emails or accurate aggregates. For monitoring, the age of the oldest unprocessed message is more meaningful than queue depth, since a large queue that drains quickly is fine, while a small one stuck is not. Alerts consider the trend of the backlog and consumer lag, so I catch a growing delay before users do.
f: Why age of oldest message over queue depth?
How do you measure message loss?

q: How do you use error budgets to negotiate with product teams about launches and risk?
p: Show the remaining budget as shared data. If healthy, product can take more risk and ship faster; if low, prioritise reliability work. The budget turns an argument into a pre-agreed rule, not a personality clash.
cmds: budget < 10%: freeze risky changes, fix reliability
tip: Present options and trade-offs, such as launching with a feature flag and staged rollout, rather than a flat no.
a: Without a shared measure, reliability debates become opinion versus opinion. The error budget gives both sides a common number. At the start of a quarter we agree the SLO and the policy. During planning, I show how much budget remains and how fast it burned recently. If there is plenty of budget, product can launch more aggressively, run experiments, or do risky migrations, because reliability has headroom. If budget is nearly spent, I recommend prioritising stability work, smaller releases or delaying a risky launch, and explain the numbers. I try to offer alternatives, not a flat refusal: use a feature flag, a canary and a staged rollout, schedule the launch for lower traffic, or do the reliability work that buys more budget first. This keeps the relationship collaborative, and the decisions follow rules the business agreed in advance.
f: How do you avoid being the blocker?
What if product disagrees with the policy?

q: What counts against the error budget and what should be excluded?
p: Count user-visible failures and slow responses from your service or its hard dependencies. Exclude client errors (4xx caused by users), synthetic probes, load tests, and agreed planned maintenance only if users were warned and the SLO document says so.
cmds: excluded: 4xx caused by client, health checks, internal test traffic
tip: Be careful with exclusions. Every exclusion makes the number look better than users' experience.
a: The budget should reflect user pain, so I count responses that failed or were too slow from the user's perspective. That includes server errors, timeouts, and requests slower than the latency threshold, whether caused by my own code or a dependency I choose to rely on. I exclude events that are not the service's fault or not real users: client errors like bad requests or unauthorised calls, health check traffic, synthetic load tests, and traffic from known abusive clients. Planned maintenance is contentious: excluding it can be justified only if users were notified and had alternatives, and if the SLO document states it. Otherwise it should count, because users still experienced downtime. Every exclusion makes the metric look better than reality, so I keep the list short, written down and reviewed, and I compare the SLI against external signals like support tickets to check that it reflects reality.
f: Should 4xx errors count?
Why be careful with planned maintenance exclusions?

q: How do you handle a single huge incident that consumes the entire quarterly error budget on day one?
p: Follow the policy: freeze risky changes, prioritise remediation, but avoid punishing the team for the whole window. Consider whether the window is too long, analyse root causes, and use shorter rolling windows and burn-rate alerts to regain balance.
cmds: review: rolling 28d window vs calendar quarter
tip: Calendar windows reset all at once; rolling windows recover gradually as the bad period ages out.
a: A large incident can use up the whole budget, and then the policy says to slow down feature work and focus on reliability. I follow it, because the rule was agreed in advance, but I apply judgement about scope. The freeze concerns risky changes, while fixes that improve reliability continue. The team completes the postmortem, delivers the highest-impact preventive actions, and demonstrates improvement before returning to normal. If the window is a calendar quarter, the team would be frozen for months on day one, which is demotivating and unrealistic, so this is a signal to consider a rolling window, such as twenty-eight days, where the bad period gradually ages out and the budget recovers. I would also check whether the SLO is calibrated correctly and whether one outage this large indicates a single point of failure that needs architectural work.
f: Why does the window type matter?
What is frozen and what continues?

q: How do you use error budget burn data in capacity and roadmap planning?
p: Track which causes consume budget (deploys, dependencies, capacity, bugs), then allocate roadmap time proportionally to the top drivers. Reliability work is justified by budget evidence instead of intuition.
tip: Label incidents with a cause category so you can sum the budget burn per category each quarter.
a: Over a quarter I tag each incident and burn event with its category, such as bad deploys, dependency failures, capacity saturation, configuration changes or unknown. Summing the consumed budget by category shows where reliability is actually lost. If thirty-eight percent of the burn comes from deployments, investing in progressive delivery, automated rollback and better pre-release testing pays off more than anything else. If a particular dependency causes a quarter of the burn, I discuss its SLO with the owning team or add fallbacks and caching. If capacity saturation is the driver, I prioritise load testing and autoscaling improvements. This evidence goes into roadmap planning as proposals with estimated budget savings, so leadership can compare reliability projects against features on a common basis. It also helps me retire work that does not move the numbers.
f: Why categorise burn by cause?
How do you justify a reliability project?

q: How would you set up fast and slow burn alerts, and what are typical window and threshold pairs?
p: Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts: page on a 14.4x burn over 1 hour (confirmed by 5 min), also 6x over 6 hours; ticket on 3x over 1 day and 1x over 3 days. The short window confirms it is still happening.
tip: A 14.4x burn over one hour consumes 2% of a 30-day budget, which justifies waking someone.
a: Burn rate is how fast I consume budget relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it over the SLO window. A burn rate of one means I will end the window at zero. The recommended approach pairs a long window with a short one. For fast, severe problems, I page when the burn rate over one hour exceeds fourteen point four, which would consume two percent of a thirty-day budget in that hour, and the five-minute rate also exceeds it, confirming the problem is still ongoing so the alert resets quickly after recovery. A second page uses six times over six hours. For slow burns that need attention but not urgently, I create tickets at three times over one day and one times over three days. This design gives high precision, good recall, and fast detection for big problems, while catching sneaky slow leaks, without relying on fixed error-rate thresholds that either flap or miss.
f: Why a short confirming window?
What does burn rate of 1 mean?

q: How do you handle on-call compensation, fairness and burnout prevention?
p: Compensate on-call time (pay or time off), limit frequency, ensure rest after night pages, distribute load fairly across time zones, track page load per person, and give engineers time to fix causes of pages.
cmds: on-call weeks per engineer per quarter
tip: If the same person is paged most often, the rotation is not fair and the system is not yet healthy.
a: On-call is a real burden, even when pages are rare, because it limits personal freedom. I treat it as work that deserves recognition through pay, time off in lieu or both, with clear policies. I keep frequency sustainable, typically no more than one week in four or five, with enough people in the rotation, and ensure people can rest after being woken at night, with a protected morning or day off. Fairness means tracking pages and out-of-hours interruptions per person and rebalancing, using follow-the-sun coverage where teams span time zones. Equally important is reducing the load: each page is a defect to fix, so I allocate time in the sprint for removing noisy alerts and repeating causes. I monitor wellbeing through surveys and one-to-ones, allow swaps and exemptions for personal circumstances, and ensure there is a backup and a clear escalation path so nobody feels alone.
f: How do you measure fairness?
How do you give recovery time?

q: What makes a good alert, and what is the test for deciding whether something should page a human?
p: A good page is urgent, actionable, user-impacting, novel and needs human judgement now. If it can wait until morning, is not actionable, or can be auto-remediated, make it a ticket, a dashboard item or automation.
cmds: test 1: does it need action in the next few minutes?
test 2: is there a known action to take (runbook link)?
test 3: is the user impact real or imminent?
tip: Every page should come with a runbook link and a clear description of impact. Otherwise the responder starts from zero.
a: I apply a simple filter before any alert pages a person. First, urgency: does it require action now, or can it wait until working hours. Second, impact: are users affected or about to be, ideally measured through symptoms like error rate and latency rather than internal causes. Third, actionability: is there something a human can usefully do, with a runbook describing diagnosis and mitigation. Fourth, novelty: if the same thing happens routinely and the fix is mechanical, automation should handle it, not a person. Alerts that fail these tests become tickets, dashboards or logs. The page itself includes the service, the impact, a link to the dashboard and the runbook, and recent changes, so the responder can begin immediately. I review alert quality in regular reviews, deleting those that never led to action and tuning those with a high false positive rate.
f: What turns a page into a ticket?
What goes in the alert message?

q: How do you structure handoffs between on-call shifts and between teams?
p: A written handoff covering open incidents, active mitigations, risky changes upcoming, noisy alerts, and follow-ups, delivered in a short sync. Use a shared log so context is not lost. Pair with a primary and secondary for continuity.
tip: Temporary silences and manual workarounds are the most dangerous items to forget in a handoff.
a: Handoffs are where context gets lost. I use a standard template that the outgoing engineer fills in: incidents still open and their current status, mitigations that are in place and must be removed, alerts that have been silenced temporarily with the reason and expiry, planned deployments or maintenance during the next shift, flaky alerts and what has been tried, and anything the person suspects might get worse. The handoff takes place in a short live conversation, not only a document, so the incoming engineer can ask questions. A running on-call log or channel keeps a history of decisions. Between teams, such as follow-the-sun, the same applies, plus explicit confirmation of ownership of any incident in progress. I use a secondary on-call as backup for continuity, and review handoff notes in retrospectives so the template improves.
f: Why a live conversation, not just a document?
What is dangerous to forget?

q: How do you design runbooks and automated remediation so on-call engineers do less manual work?
p: Start with a runbook per alert, then script the repeated steps, then wire safe, idempotent automation with guardrails, rate limits and audit logs. Promote steps from runbook to script to automatic action as confidence grows.
cmds: auto-remediate: rotate logs when disk > 85% (max 3 per hour)
tip: Add a circuit breaker to automation. A remediation that loops can make an incident much worse.
a: I think of a ladder. First there is a written runbook for each actionable alert, explaining what it means, how to diagnose, and how to mitigate. When engineers repeat the same steps, I convert them to a script that can be run with one command, with a dry run mode. The next step is a button or chat command with approvals and audit logging, usable by anyone on call. For well-understood, low-risk cases, I go to automatic remediation, such as restarting a stuck worker or rotating logs when a disk fills. Automation needs guardrails: it must be idempotent, limited in rate with a maximum number of actions per time window, produce notifications, and stop and escalate to a human when it does not work. Otherwise a flawed automation can amplify an outage. Each automated action is reviewed after use, and the underlying cause is still tracked for a permanent fix.
f: Why limit automation rates?
How do you decide what to automate first?

q: How should a team run an effective on-call retrospective or weekly alert review?
p: Review last week's pages: classify actionable vs noise, identify top sources, assign owners to fix or delete alerts, track trends in pages per shift, and celebrate reductions. Keep it short and recurring.
cmds: pages by alert name, last 7 days
time to acknowledge / resolve per page
action: delete | tune | automate | fix cause
tip: Delete aggressively. Alerts that never lead to action cost sleep and attention.
a: A weekly thirty-minute review keeps alert quality from decaying. The previous on-call engineer brings data: how many pages, which alerts fired most, which were actionable and which were noise, how long they took to resolve, and how many came out of hours. For each top item the team picks one of a few outcomes: delete the alert because it is useless, tune the threshold or add duration to reduce flapping, automate the response, or fix the underlying cause with a ticket and owner. I track the trend in pages per shift and in the percent of pages that led to meaningful action, with a goal such as at most two actionable pages per twelve-hour shift. The meeting also shares knowledge from tricky incidents and updates runbooks. Recognising and celebrating improvements reinforces the habit and keeps morale up.
f: What metrics do you bring?
What are the possible outcomes for a noisy alert?

q: How do you run an incident when the root cause is unknown and the clock is ticking?
p: Stabilise first: check recent changes, roll back, shift traffic, scale or shed load. Form hypotheses, split investigators, time-box each, and keep a timeline. Mitigation matters more than finding the cause during the incident.
cmds: git log --since='2 hours ago' --oneline  # what changed?
kubectl top pods; kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
tip: Most incidents correlate with a recent change. Roll back first, ask why later.
a: When the cause is unclear, I focus on reducing user impact, not on winning the debugging puzzle. The first question is what changed recently, because deployments, config updates, feature flags and infrastructure changes explain most incidents, and reverting is a fast, low-risk mitigation. If nothing changed, I look at the golden signals and dependency health to localise the problem, and use general mitigations like failing over to another region, scaling up, shedding load or disabling a non-essential feature. I split the team: one person investigates logs and metrics, another checks dependencies, with the incident commander coordinating and keeping a timeline. I time-box each hypothesis, say ten minutes, and rotate if it leads nowhere. Communication to stakeholders goes out regularly. Once service is restored, the deeper root cause analysis moves to the postmortem, with the evidence preserved.
f: Why roll back before diagnosing?
How do you time-box hypotheses?

q: What does an effective incident communication cadence look like for customers and executives?
p: Acknowledge quickly, state impact and what you know, give regular updates even without news, name the next update time, avoid speculation, and close with resolution and follow-up. Separate technical channels from stakeholder updates.
cmds: T+10m: 'We are investigating elevated errors in checkout. Next update 30 min.'
tip: Promise the time of the next update, then keep it, even if there is nothing new.
a: During an incident, silence creates anxiety and duplicate questions. I assign a communications lead, separate from the technical responders, so engineers can focus. The first public message goes out quickly, acknowledging the problem, describing the user-visible impact in plain language, and saying when the next update will come. Then I update on that cadence, usually every thirty minutes for severe incidents, even if the update is only that we are still working on it. Messages state what we know, what we are doing, and avoid guessing about cause or promising a time to fix. Internal executives get a slightly more detailed update with business impact, the status of mitigation, and any decisions needed. When resolved, I send a clear closure message and later share a summary or postmortem. A status page, templates and a defined owner make this repeatable under stress.
f: Why a separate communications lead?
What should you avoid saying mid-incident?

q: How do you handle an incident that spans multiple teams or vendors, with unclear ownership?
p: Declare a single incident commander, open one shared channel and bridge, list involved parties and owners, assign tasks explicitly, escalate vendors through support contracts, and keep one timeline. Resolve ownership debates after the incident.
cmds: roles: IC, Ops lead, Comms lead, Scribe
vendor: open P1 case, request named engineer, share evidence
tip: The incident commander has authority to assign work. Arguing over ownership is for the postmortem.
a: With many parties, the main risk is confusion: duplicated work, conflicting changes and nobody in charge. I establish a single incident commander who coordinates and has the authority to make decisions, a single channel and call for everyone, and named leads for each affected area. A scribe keeps one timeline so decisions and observations are recorded. Tasks are assigned to specific people with a time to report back. For a vendor, I open the highest-priority support case immediately, escalate through our account contact, supply logs and a clear description of symptoms and our evidence, and ask for a named engineer, while preparing my own mitigation in case they are slow, such as failing over to another provider. If it is unclear who owns a component, the commander assigns someone to take it for now, and the ownership question is addressed in the postmortem.
f: How do you escalate with a vendor?
Who decides when ownership is unclear?

q: What is the difference between an incident commander and a technical lead, and why separate them?
p: The incident commander coordinates, decides, delegates and communicates; the technical lead dives into diagnosis and fixes. Separating roles prevents the person debugging from losing the big picture and keeps coordination continuous.
cmds: IC: owns process, priorities, decisions, delegation
Ops/Tech lead: hands-on diagnosis and mitigation
tip: If you are the IC, resist the urge to debug. Your job is to keep everyone effective.
a: The incident commander manages the response as a whole: understanding the current state, deciding priorities, assigning tasks, requesting additional help, ensuring communication happens, and deciding when to escalate or declare the incident over. The technical lead, or ops lead, works hands-on with the systems: investigating logs, testing hypotheses, performing mitigations. Combining the roles is a common failure, because when the same person goes deep into a technical problem, nobody tracks the broader picture, updates stop, and other responders wait for direction. In small incidents one person may hold several roles, but as severity grows I split them. The commander should be the person best at coordination and staying calm, not necessarily the most senior engineer or the one who knows the system best. Regular practice in game days builds this muscle, and handing off the commander role during long incidents prevents fatigue.
f: Who should be the commander?
How do you hand off command?

q: How do you decide to roll back versus roll forward during a bad deploy?
p: Roll back when the change is clearly implicated and rollback is safe and fast. Roll forward when rollback is risky (schema changes, data migrations) or the fix is tiny and well understood. Decide on time to restore and risk.
cmds: # data migration applied? check backward compatibility first
tip: Design deploys to be backward compatible so rollback is always possible. Expand, then migrate, then contract.
a: My default is to roll back, because it restores a known good state quickly and is predictable. Before I do it, I check the rollback is safe: has a database migration already run that the old version cannot handle, has data been written in a new format, have other services started depending on the new behaviour. If so, rolling back might make things worse, and a forward fix may be safer. Roll forward is also reasonable when the cause is clear and the fix is a trivial, well-tested change that can pass through the pipeline faster than a rollback, though in a real incident I am cautious about untested rushed fixes. I compare estimated time to restore for each option and the risk of making things worse. To keep rollback always possible, I design changes to be backward compatible, using expand-and-contract migrations and feature flags, so the old version works with the new schema.
f: When is rollback unsafe?
What is expand and contract?

q: How do you write postmortem action items that actually reduce recurrence?
p: Make actions specific, owned, time-bound and prioritised by impact: prevent, detect and mitigate. Prefer systemic fixes and automation over reminders and training. Track them in the same backlog as feature work.
cmds: P0 prevent: add schema validation in CI (owner: Priya, due: 2 wks)
P1 detect: alert on queue age > 5 min (owner: Sam, due: 1 wk)
P2 mitigate: automate rollback on error spike (owner: Lee, due: 6 wks)
tip: If the action is 'tell people to be careful', the system is still unsafe. Fix the system, not people.
a: Weak action items like be more careful or send a reminder do not change a system. Good ones address how the failure happened and are concrete: a code change, an alert, a guardrail in the pipeline, a test, or a design change. I classify them as preventing recurrence, improving detection, and reducing impact when it happens again, and prioritise by the risk they reduce versus effort. Each item has a named owner, a due date and a ticket in the team's normal backlog, not a separate document that gets forgotten, and the postmortem links to them. I limit the number to what the team can actually complete, and mark the one or two critical items as must-do. Progress is reviewed in a regular meeting, and completion rates are reported. If an action keeps slipping, I escalate or explicitly decide not to do it and record the accepted risk.
f: What are the three types of actions?
What do you do with slipping actions?

q: How do you facilitate a blameless postmortem meeting when emotions are high or someone made an obvious error?
p: Set ground rules, focus on how the system allowed the error, use neutral language and timeline reconstruction, ask what made the action reasonable at the time, and keep leaders from assigning blame. Safety encourages honesty.
cmds: ask: 'What did you know at the time?'
ask: 'What made this decision seem reasonable?'
replace 'human error' with the missing guardrail
tip: If people fear punishment, they hide details, and you lose the information needed to prevent recurrence.
a: I open the meeting by restating that the goal is learning and that we assume everyone acted with good intent given what they knew. I walk through the timeline from logs and chat records, rather than memories, so the discussion is factual. When someone made a mistake, I ask questions about context: what information did you have, what did the dashboards show, what made that choice reasonable, what was confusing. This shifts attention to missing guardrails, unclear tooling, poor documentation or pressure. I avoid asking why did you, which sounds accusatory, and I replace phrases like human error with the system gap that allowed it. If senior leaders attend, I brief them beforehand not to assign fault. The person involved is invited, not forced, to share their perspective. When people feel safe, they share the full picture, which is the only way to find real contributing factors.
f: Why avoid asking 'why did you'?
How do you handle leaders who want accountability?

q: What is a good timeline in a postmortem and how do you build it from evidence?
p: A timestamped sequence in one time zone covering detection, escalation, key decisions, mitigations and recovery, built from logs, metrics, chat and deploy records, with gaps and uncertainty marked. It shows both what happened and what people believed.
tip: Include decision points and what responders believed, not only system events. That reveals why actions made sense.
a: I build the timeline from objective sources: monitoring graphs, deployment and change logs, alert histories, and the incident channel transcript, all converted to a single time zone. I record key events in order: when the problem began, when it was detected and how, when people were paged, hypotheses tried, mitigations applied, and the recovery time. Importantly I add the responders' beliefs and decision points, such as at fourteen twenty we thought the database was the cause, because that explains why certain steps were taken and what information was missing. I mark uncertain items and gaps instead of guessing. The timeline allows me to compute durations like time to detect, time to engage and time to mitigate, which show where the process can improve. Reviewing it with the people involved corrects errors and often uncovers details that were not recorded anywhere.
f: What metrics come from a timeline?
Why record what responders believed?

q: How do you handle postmortems for incidents caused by a third-party vendor or cloud provider outage?
p: Focus on what you control: detection, your dependency design, fallback options, communication and contract follow-up. Examine why a single provider failure had that impact and what resilience investments are justified.
cmds: question: why was this a single point of failure?
question: did our alerts detect it before the vendor status page?
question: could we have failed over or degraded gracefully?
action: request provider RCA, review SLA credits
tip: Blaming the vendor ends learning. The question is how your system should behave when a dependency fails.
a: Even when the root cause lies with a provider, the incident revealed something about my system: it depended on that component in a way that turned the failure into user impact. So the postmortem examines my side. Did we detect the problem quickly ourselves or only learn from the vendor status page? Could we have degraded gracefully, served cached data, switched to a secondary region or provider, or queued work? Was our communication to customers clear and timely? What did the dependency's published SLA promise versus our own commitments? I request the provider's root cause analysis and follow up on contractual remedies such as service credits, but I treat those as secondary. Then I evaluate whether investment in redundancy, such as multi-region or multi-provider, is justified by the cost of outages and the likelihood, rather than reflexively adding complexity.
f: Should you always go multi-provider?
What do you ask the vendor for?

q: How do you share postmortem learnings across a large organisation so other teams benefit?
p: Publish postmortems in a searchable internal repository, hold regular review sessions, summarise themes in newsletters, tag by cause and component, and turn recurring lessons into checklists, templates and platform guardrails.
tip: The best sharing mechanism is a guardrail in the platform that prevents the same failure for everyone.
a: Learning only helps if it travels. I publish every significant postmortem in a central, searchable repository with consistent tags for cause, affected component and customer impact, so people can look up similar failures before designing something. A regular cross-team reading or review session, perhaps monthly, discusses a few of the most interesting incidents, which builds a shared culture and spreads knowledge informally. I also analyse across postmortems to find patterns, such as repeated configuration-change failures, and report themes to leadership with suggested investments. The most scalable step is converting lessons into defaults: add a check to the deployment pipeline, update service templates and production readiness checklists, build a library that handles retries safely, or enforce a policy. Then every team benefits without needing to read the document. Summaries and newsletters help keep awareness high, without blame.
f: How do you find cross-incident patterns?
What is the most scalable form of sharing?

q: Give examples of toil and non-toil, and explain the criteria that define toil.
p: Toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical work with no enduring value that scales linearly with service growth. Examples: manual restarts, ticket-driven provisioning. Not toil: writing automation, design, postmortems, one-off migrations.
cmds: toil: manually rotating certificates every quarter
toil: approving access requests by hand
toil: restarting a leaking service nightly
not toil: building self-service access tooling
tip: The key question is whether the work leaves the system permanently better. Toil does not.
a: Toil has several characteristics: it is manual, repetitive, could be automated, is tactical and interrupt-driven rather than strategic, produces no lasting improvement, and grows in proportion to the size or traffic of the service. Examples include manually rotating certificates on a schedule, handling routine access requests by hand, restarting a leaking process every night, manually copying data between systems, and responding to alerts with the same fixed procedure each time. Work that looks like operations but is not toil includes designing and writing the automation that eliminates the above, performing a one-off migration, writing a postmortem, tuning capacity models, or on-call incident investigations that teach something new. Overhead like meetings and administration is also not toil, though it is not engineering. Identifying toil precisely matters because the aim is to keep it below a threshold and systematically remove it.
f: Is a one-off migration toil?
Why does scale-linearity matter?

q: How do you quantify the ROI of automating a task, and when is it not worth it?
p: Compare annual time saved (frequency x duration x people) plus error reduction against development and maintenance cost. Skip automation for rare, quick or unstable tasks, or when removing the need is better than automating it.
cmds: also: risk reduction, faster lead time
tip: Sometimes the best fix is to eliminate the task entirely by changing the process or design, not automate it.
a: I estimate the recurring cost of the manual work: how often it happens, how long it takes, and how many people are involved, converted into hours per year. I add intangible benefits such as fewer errors, faster response for users, and less interruption. Then I estimate the cost to build the automation plus its ongoing maintenance, because scripts rot. If the payback period is short, say under a year, and the task is stable, automation is a clear win. It is not worth it when the task is rare, takes minutes, or the underlying process is likely to change soon. Also, I first ask whether the task should exist at all: sometimes removing an approval step or fixing the root cause of why the task is needed gives a bigger gain than automating it. Cheap partial automation, like a script with a checklist, can capture most of the value.
f: Why include maintenance cost?
When should you eliminate rather than automate?

q: What is a self-service platform's role in reducing toil, and how do you measure adoption?
p: Self-service lets developers provision and operate resources through APIs or templates without tickets, removing SRE from the critical path. Measure adoption, ticket volume, time to provision and satisfaction.
tip: A self-service tool nobody uses just moved the toil to its builders. Treat the platform as a product.
a: Many operational tasks are requests from developers: create a database, add a queue, get a new environment, change DNS. If each needs a ticket and manual work from SRE, toil grows with the number of teams. A self-service platform, such as templates, a portal or declarative APIs with guardrails built in, lets developers do these tasks safely themselves in minutes, and encodes security and reliability best practice by default. I measure its success with the number of related tickets, the time to provision before and after, the percentage of services using the standard path, and developer satisfaction. I treat the platform as a product: talk to users, publish documentation, keep a roadmap and measure reliability of the platform itself. Without adoption, the effort is wasted, so I prioritise the most requested and most painful workflows first.
f: How do you measure platform success?
What guardrails belong in self-service?

q: How do you tackle toil that comes from a poorly designed or legacy system that nobody dares to change?
p: Quantify the cost, add observability and tests as a safety net, carve out the worst pain with strangler-style improvements, get management support with data, and avoid big-bang rewrites. Reduce toil incrementally.
cmds: toil log: 14 h/week on manual reconciliation
step 2: automate the top 2 manual steps
step 3: replace one module behind an interface
tip: Characterisation tests record what the legacy system does today, giving courage to change it.
a: Fear of changing a legacy system usually stems from poor visibility and no tests. So I start by making the cost visible: record the hours spent per week and the incidents it causes, so I can build a business case. Next I create a safety net: add monitoring to understand real behaviour, and write characterisation tests that capture current outputs, even if imperfect, so I can detect unintended changes. Then I attack the most painful manual steps with small automations that wrap the system without modifying its core, and gradually replace components behind stable interfaces using a strangler approach, routing a growing share of work to the new implementation. I avoid a big-bang rewrite, which tends to be late and risky. Each increment must deliver measurable toil reduction, which keeps stakeholder support and demonstrates progress.
f: What is a characterisation test?
Why avoid big-bang rewrites?

q: How do you design retry policies safely, including retry budgets and idempotency keys?
p: Retry only transient, idempotent operations with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, and use a retry budget (percentage of requests) to prevent amplification. Use idempotency keys for non-idempotent writes like payments.
cmds: retry on: 503, 504, connect timeout; never on 400, 401, 404
tip: Retries across several layers multiply: three layers with three attempts each make 27 calls for one failure.
a: Retries help with transient errors but can turn a small problem into an outage. I retry only when the error is likely temporary, such as a connection timeout or a service unavailable response, never for client errors. Each retry uses exponential backoff with random jitter, so clients spread out instead of synchronising, with a small maximum attempt count and an overall deadline. To avoid amplification, I use a retry budget, which limits retries to a fraction of normal traffic, say ten percent, so that a struggling service is not flooded. I also watch for retries at multiple layers multiplying, so I set them at one layer where possible. For operations that change state, such as creating a payment, retries are only safe if the operation is idempotent, so I require an idempotency key that the server uses to deduplicate. Circuit breakers stop retries entirely when failure is persistent.
f: Why does jitter matter?
What is a retry budget?

q: What is a service mesh's contribution to reliability, and what costs does it add?
p: A mesh provides consistent retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, mTLS, traffic shifting and telemetry outside application code. Costs: extra latency and resource use, operational complexity, and another critical failure domain.
tip: Adopt a mesh for a clear problem, such as mTLS or uniform traffic policy, not because it is fashionable.
a: A service mesh puts a proxy next to each workload, so cross-cutting reliability features are implemented uniformly without changing every application: timeouts, retries with limits, circuit breaking and outlier ejection, load balancing, canary traffic splitting, fault injection for testing, mutual TLS between services, and rich metrics and traces for every call. That consistency is valuable in organisations with many languages and teams. The costs are real: each hop adds proxy latency and memory and CPU overhead, the control plane becomes critical infrastructure whose outage or bad configuration can break everything, upgrades are complex, and debugging requires understanding another layer. Teams must learn its configuration model. I adopt a mesh when there is a clear need such as zero-trust encryption or uniform traffic management at scale, start with a limited rollout, have strong observability of the mesh itself, and keep an escape hatch to bypass it.
f: What new failure modes does it introduce?
When is a mesh overkill?

q: How do you design a graceful shutdown and connection draining for zero-downtime deploys?
p: On SIGTERM, fail readiness so traffic stops, finish in-flight requests within a grace period, close connections cleanly, and use preStop delay to let load balancers deregister. Match terminationGracePeriod to the longest request.
tip: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM race each other. The preStop sleep covers the propagation delay.
a: Deployments fail in subtle ways when pods are killed while serving requests. A correct shutdown sequence has several parts. When the orchestrator decides to stop a pod, it removes it from the service endpoints and sends a termination signal, but these propagate asynchronously, so some traffic may still arrive for a few seconds. A short pre-stop delay gives load balancers time to stop routing. On receiving the signal, the application stops accepting new connections, marks itself not ready, completes in-flight requests within a deadline, flushes buffers and closes database connections, then exits. The termination grace period must be longer than the longest request plus the delay, or the process is force-killed. Long-lived connections like websockets need a mechanism to ask clients to reconnect elsewhere. I test this under load during rollouts, watching for error spikes, and verify that jobs and consumers also stop cleanly and release leases.
f: Why a preStop sleep?
What happens to long-lived connections?

q: How do you build and test a disaster recovery plan for a stateful service, including RTO and RPO targets?
p: Define business RTO/RPO, choose a strategy (backup-restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active) by cost, automate failover and restore, and test regularly with real restores. An untested backup is not a backup.
cmds: dr drill: failover region, run smoke tests, fail back
tip: Measure the real restore time and data loss in a drill, then compare it with the target.
a: I start from business requirements: how long can the service be down, the recovery time objective, and how much data can we lose, the recovery point objective. Those numbers drive the strategy and cost: backup and restore is cheapest but slowest; pilot light keeps minimal infrastructure ready; warm standby runs a scaled-down copy; active-active gives near-zero downtime at the highest cost and complexity. For stateful data, replication and continuous log shipping set the recovery point, while automation of provisioning and failover sets the recovery time. I document runbooks, keep infrastructure as code so the environment can be rebuilt, store backups in a separate account or region with immutability, and monitor backup success. The key is testing: scheduled drills that restore from backups, run verification queries and a failover to the secondary, measuring actual times against targets and fixing gaps. I include failback and dependency ordering in the exercise.
f: How do RTO and RPO differ?
Why store backups in a separate account?

q: What is a feature flag's role in reliability, and what are the risks of flags themselves?
p: Flags allow gradual rollout, kill switches and fast mitigation without redeploys. Risks: stale flags, untested combinations, flag service outages, and config errors. Mitigate with defaults, expiry, ownership and testing.
cmds: kill switch: disable feature in seconds
default if flag service down: safe/off
tip: Define safe defaults so a flag service outage does not take your application down.
a: Feature flags decouple deploying code from enabling behaviour. For reliability this offers a gradual rollout to a small percentage of users with monitoring, immediate disabling of a problematic feature without a rollback or deployment, and operational switches that shed non-essential load during overload. The risks come from the flags themselves. They add code paths whose combinations are rarely all tested; they accumulate as dead code if not removed; the flag management service can become a dependency, so the application needs cached values and safe defaults if it is unreachable; and a mistaken change to a flag is itself a production change that can cause an outage, so it needs review, audit logs and ideally staged propagation. I assign each flag an owner and expiry date, remove it after full rollout, and treat flag changes with the same care as deployments.
f: What are safe defaults?
Why give flags an expiry?

q: How do you run chaos experiments in Kubernetes using tools like Chaos Mesh or Litmus?
p: Define steady-state metrics, write an experiment manifest (pod kill, network delay, CPU stress), scope by label and namespace, run during working hours with abort conditions, and observe whether SLOs hold. Start in staging.
cmds: apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1 kind: NetworkChaos spec: action: delay delay: { latency: 200ms } selector: { labelSelectors: { app: payments } } duration: 5m
tip: Always have a one-command abort and automatic stop conditions tied to SLO alerts.
a: I begin by defining the hypothesis and steady state, for example that when one payments pod is killed, error rate stays below one percent and latency within target. Then I write the experiment declaratively with a tool like Chaos Mesh or Litmus: choose the fault type such as killing pods, adding network latency or loss, stressing CPU or memory, or partitioning a dependency, and restrict the blast radius with namespace and label selectors, a small percentage of targets, and a short duration. I run first in a staging environment, then in production with care, during working hours, with the team watching dashboards, and with automatic abort conditions linked to alerts. After the run, I compare observed behaviour with the hypothesis, record findings, fix weaknesses such as missing retries or bad timeouts, and repeat the experiment to confirm. Over time I schedule experiments continuously as regression tests.
f: What is a good first experiment?
How do you limit blast radius?

q: What kinds of failures reveal the most in distributed systems: latency injection or crashes? Why is slowness harder?
p: Slowness is harder than crashes because it ties up threads, queues and connections, triggers retries and cascades, and evades health checks. Latency injection exposes missing timeouts, bulkheads and backpressure.
cmds: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 500ms 100ms
toxiproxy-cli toxic add -t latency -a latency=1000 db_proxy
kubectl exec pod -- tc qdisc del dev eth0 root
# watch: thread pool saturation, queue depth, p99
tip: A dead dependency fails fast. A slow one holds your resources hostage.
a: A crashed dependency produces immediate errors, which are easy to detect and handle with retries or fallbacks. A slow dependency is far more dangerous: callers wait, holding threads, connections and memory; queues build; retries pile on more load; health checks may still pass because the process is alive. This can exhaust resources in upstream services and cascade through the system. So latency injection reveals missing or too generous timeouts, absent bulkheads that should isolate resource pools, lack of circuit breakers, and poor backpressure. Packet loss, partial failures and intermittent errors reveal similar weaknesses. I prefer to inject gradual slowness at the network or proxy level, for example adding hundreds of milliseconds to a database call, and observe thread pool usage, queue depth and tail latency. The fix is usually layered: timeouts, bulkheads, load shedding, circuit breaking and graceful degradation.
f: Why is slowness worse than failure?
What protects against slow dependencies?

q: How do you verify that failover works for databases and caches without causing a real outage?
p: Rehearse in staging and then production in a controlled window: trigger managed failover, measure client reconnect behaviour, confirm no data loss, and check connection pool and DNS cache handling. Run regularly so it is routine.
tip: Applications often fail not because failover is slow but because they cache DNS or hold dead connections.
a: Failover is only trustworthy if exercised. I schedule controlled failover drills, first in a production-like staging environment and then in production during low-risk windows with the team ready. I trigger the managed failover or kill the primary, then observe: how long until the replica is promoted, how clients behave when connections break, whether connection pools detect dead connections and reconnect, whether DNS time-to-live and client-side caching delay the switch, and whether any writes were lost or duplicated. I measure the real recovery time against the target and check dashboards for error spikes and queue build-up. Typical findings include applications with infinite retries, no connection validation, long DNS caching, or sessions that are lost. I fix them, repeat the drill, and then keep it on a regular schedule so that the team stays practised and regressions get caught.
f: What commonly goes wrong in failover?
Why repeat the drill regularly?

q: How do you build a resilience scorecard or maturity model for services?
p: Define criteria like SLOs, tested failover, timeouts, runbooks, capacity tests, dependency maps and chaos testing, score each service, share results, and use them to prioritise investment and gate launches.
tip: Use scorecards to guide improvement, not to shame teams. Show progress over time.
a: A scorecard turns resilience from a vague aspiration into a checklist that teams can improve. I define a set of criteria drawn from experience, such as a documented SLO with burn alerts, timeouts and retries configured properly, graceful degradation for non-critical dependencies, tested failover, backups with verified restores, a load test within the last quarter, runbooks linked from alerts, a dependency map, and periodic chaos experiments. Each service is scored against the criteria, perhaps in levels from basic to advanced, and results are presented on a dashboard. Leadership uses it to see where risk is concentrated and to prioritise investment; teams use it as a roadmap of concrete next steps. I make the criteria proportionate to service tier, since an internal tool needs less than a payment system. To keep it constructive, I focus on trends and support, and use it as a production readiness gate for new critical services.
f: Why scale criteria by tier?
How do you avoid shaming teams?

q: How do you perform capacity planning for a database, including connection limits, IOPS and storage growth?
p: Track CPU, memory, IOPS, connections, replication lag and storage growth; project trends with headroom; load test; plan scaling steps (vertical, read replicas, sharding) well before limits, considering lead time.
tip: Connection limits are often hit before CPU. Pooling is usually the first and cheapest capacity fix.
a: Databases are hard to scale quickly, so I plan early. I monitor the main resources: CPU and memory, disk IOPS and throughput, connection counts, replication lag, cache hit ratio, and storage consumption. I project trends, for example linear growth of storage over the past thirty days into the next ninety, and define alert thresholds that give enough lead time to act, considering how long a resize, migration or new replica takes. Connection limits are an easy trap because each application instance opens pools; a connection pooler such as PgBouncer reduces pressure. I load test with realistic queries to find the point of saturation and to validate that indexes and queries are efficient before simply adding hardware. Scaling options include vertical upgrades, read replicas and caching for read-heavy workloads, partitioning, and eventually sharding for write scale. I also plan for peak events and keep headroom for failover, when one node must carry the load.
f: Why do connection limits matter?
What gives you scaling lead time?

q: What are the pitfalls of autoscaling on CPU alone, and which better signals exist?
p: CPU lags and doesn't reflect I/O-bound or queue-driven work. Better signals: request rate per pod, queue depth or age, concurrency, latency, or custom business metrics, plus scale-up speed and warm-up considerations.
cmds: keda: ScaledObject triggers: - type: kafka metadata: { lagThreshold: "100" }
metrics: - type: Pods pods: { metric: { name: requests_per_second }, target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "50" } }
tip: Scale on a leading indicator of load, not a lagging indicator of pain.
a: CPU is a convenient default but often a poor trigger. It lags behind demand, so by the time CPU is high, users already see latency. It also misrepresents workloads that are I/O bound, waiting on databases, or driven by queues, where CPU stays low while latency climbs. Better signals reflect work arriving or waiting: requests per second per instance, concurrent in-flight requests, queue depth or the age of the oldest message, or consumer lag for streaming workloads. Event-driven autoscalers can scale on these metrics, and even down to zero for sporadic jobs. I also consider the mechanics: startup and warm-up time, image pull time, scale-up rate limits, and stabilisation windows to avoid flapping. I keep minimum replicas for baseline resilience, set maximums to protect dependencies and budgets, and load test to confirm that the autoscaler keeps latency within target during a ramp.
f: Why is CPU a lagging indicator?
What is KEDA used for?

q: How do you use load shedding priority and admission control to keep critical traffic working during overload?
p: Classify requests by criticality, reject or queue lower-priority work first when saturation signals appear, return fast errors with retry hints, and protect resources for critical paths. Overload control should be automatic and tested.
cmds: if inflight > limit: shed batch, then normal
tip: Failing fast with a clear error is better than slow timeouts that hold resources and make everything worse.
a: When demand exceeds capacity, trying to serve everything means serving nothing well: queues grow, latency rises and requests time out, wasting work. Load shedding deliberately rejects some work to keep the rest healthy. I classify traffic by importance: user-facing checkout is critical, background sync and analytics are lower. Detection uses saturation signals such as concurrent requests, queue length, memory pressure or latency. When thresholds are crossed, the service rejects the lowest priority requests first with a quick error and a hint to retry later, then progressively more, while reserving capacity for critical flows. Clients are expected to honour the retry hint with backoff so that shedding does not trigger a storm. Adaptive concurrency limits can set thresholds automatically. I test with load generators that push beyond capacity to confirm that the service degrades gracefully, and publish metrics on shed requests so I can tune.
f: What should the client do when shed?
How do you pick what to shed first?

q: How do you account for cost in capacity decisions, such as spot instances, reservations and rightsizing?
p: Match purchase model to workload: reserved or committed for baseline, on-demand for variable, spot for fault-tolerant batch. Rightsize using utilisation data, but keep headroom for failure and spikes, and track unit costs.
cmds: kubectl top nodes; kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=cpu
tip: Cost per unit of work (per request, per user) is more useful than the raw bill when traffic grows.
a: Capacity is a trade-off between reliability and cost. I separate demand into a steady baseline, which I cover with reserved or committed capacity at a discount, and variable load, which uses on-demand instances or autoscaling. Fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads such as batch jobs, CI runners and stateless workers can run on spot capacity at a large discount, as long as they handle interruptions and are spread across instance types and zones. Rightsizing uses real utilisation data to shrink oversized instances and requests, but I preserve headroom for traffic spikes, deployments and the loss of a zone, so that I do not trade resilience for savings. I track unit economics, such as cost per thousand requests, to see efficiency as the system grows, and review commitments regularly. Cost data is shared with teams, creating accountability, and reliability targets stay the guardrail.
f: What workloads suit spot instances?
Why track cost per request?

q: Your service's error rate jumps to 30% right after a deploy, but the canary looked healthy. What could explain this and what do you do?
p: Mitigate: roll back. Then investigate why the canary missed it: low traffic share, wrong traffic type, delayed effect (cache expiry, connection pool, background job), config differences, or a dependency that only fails at full volume.
cmds: compare canary vs prod: traffic %, endpoints hit, data sets
check cache TTLs, cron jobs, feature flag segments
tip: A canary is only as good as the traffic it sees. If it never exercised the failing path, it proved nothing.
a: First I restore service by rolling back, since the deploy is the obvious suspect and rollback is fast. Then I work out why the canary gave false confidence. Possibilities include: the canary received too small a share of traffic or too short an observation time, so rare paths or heavy users were not exercised; the failing code path depends on a specific customer segment, endpoint or data shape not in the sample; the effect is delayed, such as a cache entry expiring, a memory leak, a connection pool filling, or a scheduled job running later; the canary and full rollout differ in configuration or in the dependencies they hit; or a downstream system only saturates at full volume. I examine the metrics comparing canary and baseline, check the failing requests, and reproduce in staging. Improvements include longer bake time, automated analysis against SLO metrics, traffic mirroring, and tests covering the failing path.
f: Why can a canary pass but full rollout fail?
How would you improve canary analysis?

q: You get paged at 3 a.m. for a database CPU alert on a service you do not know well. How do you proceed?
p: Check user impact first, open the runbook, look at recent changes and top queries, mitigate (kill runaway queries, scale, shed load), escalate to the owning team if needed, and document what you did for handoff.
cmds: select pid, state, now()-query_start as dur, left(query,80) from pg_stat_activity where state<>'idle' order by dur desc limit 10;
tip: Escalating early when you lack context is a strength. The cost of waking a colleague is lower than a prolonged outage.
a: At 3 a.m. I start by assessing whether users are impacted: error rate, latency and the service's SLO dashboards. The alert description should link to a runbook, so I follow it. I check what changed recently, deployments, migrations or traffic spikes, and look at the database's active queries to see whether a few expensive or runaway statements are driving CPU. If I find an obvious offender, I can cancel the query, and if a recent change is implicated, I roll it back. If load is simply high, I consider mitigation like scaling the instance, adding capacity to read replicas, enabling caching or shedding non-critical traffic. If I do not know the service and the runbook is insufficient, I escalate to the secondary or the service owner without hesitation. I write down my actions in the incident channel, and after resolution I improve the runbook and file follow-up tickets.
f: When do you escalate?
What do you record while mitigating?

q: A marketing campaign will send 10x normal traffic next Tuesday and you were told on Friday. How do you prepare in four days?
p: Quantify expected load, load test critical paths, pre-scale and raise limits, warm caches, protect dependencies, add load shedding and a kill switch, brief on-call, set up a war room and rehearse rollback.
cmds: pre-warm: CDN cache, DB connection pool, JIT
tip: Check quotas and third-party rate limits. They are the usual hidden ceiling in a surge.
a: First I clarify expectations with marketing: expected peak requests, user journeys, timing, and the risks if we fail. Then I translate that into capacity needs and identify the critical path, such as landing page, search and checkout. I load test those paths in a production-like environment up to and beyond twelve times current traffic to find bottlenecks, and fix the biggest ones: database queries, cache usage, connection pools. I check hard limits that cannot be changed quickly, cloud quotas, third-party API rate limits and payment provider capacity, and request increases now. Before the event I pre-scale instances and databases, warm caches and CDN, and configure autoscaling with higher maximums. I add protections: rate limiting, priority load shedding, and a feature kill switch for non-essential components. On the day, on-call is staffed with a war room, dashboards and a rollback plan, and a clear communication channel with marketing.
f: What is the hidden ceiling in a surge?
How do you decide what to shed?

q: A chaos experiment accidentally causes a customer-visible outage. How do you respond and what changes?
p: Abort the experiment immediately, restore service, communicate honestly, run a blameless postmortem, review blast radius, abort conditions and approvals, and keep the practice with stronger safeguards rather than abandoning it.
cmds: verify steady state restored: error rate, latency
postmortem: why was blast radius larger than planned?
new guard: auto-abort on SLO burn > 2x
tip: The experiment revealed a real weakness. The failure is valuable if you learn and tighten the process.
a: The first step is to stop the experiment and restore service, using the abort mechanism I prepared and any standard incident response. I treat it like any other incident: communicate with affected customers and stakeholders honestly, noting that it was caused by our own testing. Afterwards I run a blameless postmortem to answer specific questions. Was the blast radius larger than planned, and why? Did the abort conditions or monitoring fail to trigger? Was the experiment approved and scheduled appropriately, with the right people watching? Did it reveal a genuine hidden dependency or weakness, which is in effect the purpose of the exercise but at too high a cost? Based on the findings I strengthen guardrails: smaller scope, automatic aborts tied to SLO burn, stricter review, running at quieter times, and more testing in staging. I keep the practice going, because abandoning it leaves such weaknesses to be discovered by real failures.
f: What guardrails would you add?
Why not stop chaos engineering?

q: Your team's toil is at 70% and leadership wants new features supported. How do you restore balance?
p: Measure and categorise toil, pick the top two sources by hours, propose time-boxed automation with expected payback, negotiate to cap new onboarding, hand back or stop supporting low-value services, and report progress.
cmds: top: access requests 12h, cert renewals 8h, manual deploys 7h
plan: self-service access (3 wks), cert-manager (2 wks)
negotiate: pause new service onboarding until toil < 50%
tip: Present it as a business trade-off with numbers: hours lost, incidents caused, and what automation will return.
a: I start by quantifying: for a couple of weeks the team records toil by category and hours, so I have data rather than feelings. I identify the few sources that account for most of the time, for example access requests, certificate renewals and manual deployments, and estimate the cost of automating each against hours saved. I take this to leadership as a trade-off. At seventy percent toil, the team has little capacity for engineering, so new feature support will degrade reliability and increase burnout. I propose a time-boxed plan to automate the top items, with expected payback, and ask for temporary measures: pause onboarding of new services, push back or hand back low-value operational work, or add headcount. I protect engineering time in each sprint, track the toil percentage each month, and share wins. If the trend does not improve, I escalate with evidence.
f: How do you gather toil data?
What do you ask leadership for?

q: Your SLO dashboard shows 99.95% but customers are complaining about slowness and errors. What could be wrong?
p: The SLI does not reflect user experience: wrong measurement point, averaged latency, excluded traffic, missing client-side failures, regional or segment issues hidden in the aggregate, or good-event definition too lenient.
cmds: compare: server-side vs client-side (RUM) success rate
break down SLI by region, customer, endpoint, device
check latency threshold vs real user tolerance
tip: Cross-check SLIs against support tickets and RUM. If they disagree, trust the customers and fix the metric.
a: A healthy dashboard with unhappy customers means the indicator is not capturing reality. I check several possibilities. The measurement point may be too far from the user, such as inside the service, missing problems at the CDN, DNS, network or client; real user monitoring would show them. Aggregation may hide a segment: a specific region, large customer or endpoint can be failing badly while the global ratio looks fine, so I break the data down. Latency may be measured as an average or against a threshold that is too generous compared with what users tolerate. Exclusions or the valid-events filter may remove traffic that users care about, like retries or certain error codes. The definition of good may count a response as successful even if the content is wrong. I compare with support tickets and synthetic probes, correct the SLI definition, and recalculate the historical numbers.
f: Why compare with RUM?
How can aggregation hide problems?
